one_liner: Young Rust io_uring reverse proxy claiming 2.05-2.30x nginx's HTTP/1.1 proxy throughput on a 2-vCPU WSL2 box.
what_it_does: Arc Gateway is a Linux-only L7 reverse proxy and API gateway (single binary arc-gateway) that terminates HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and TLS (rustls) and forwards to upstream pools, with radix-tree routing, GCRA rate limiting (optionally Redis-backed), Wasmtime plugins, traffic mirroring, ACME, XDP/eBPF filtering and Prometheus metrics. It is configured with its own JSON/TOML/YAML file rather than nginx.conf, so it replaces nginx's proxy role but is not a drop-in for nginx configuration or its static-file, caching and module ecosystem.
how_it_is_fast: Thread-per-core workers each own an io_uring ring (custom bindings in arc-net), a registered fixed-buffer pool and a connection slab, with multishot accept and optional SQPOLL, so the hot path batches socket I/O into few kernel transitions and avoids cross-thread locks. HTTP/1.1 heads are parsed in place in the fixed buffers and responses are forwarded from the same buffer, and upstream connections are pooled per worker. The project gives no profile or ablation showing which of these produces the reported gap over nginx's epoll workers.
when_to_use: Experimenting with an io_uring, thread-per-core Rust proxy on Linux 6.1+ where small-response HTTP/1.1 proxy throughput per core is the main goal and you can run your own wrk comparison against your nginx config.
Lab or edge setups that want gateway features (GCRA rate limiting, WASM request plugins, traffic mirroring, XDP SYN-flood filtering) in one Rust binary rather than nginx plus modules.
Reading a compact, single-author example of io_uring fixed buffers, multishot accept and per-worker upstream pools in Rust.
when_not_to_use: Production traffic: 11 commits between 2026-03-01 and 2026-03-11, 8 stars, releases v0.1.1 and v0.1.2, and the README itself says the project is 'in active testing'; fixes for self-upstream loops, HEAD handling and async upstream I/O landed after the benchmark numbers were published.
TLS-heavy serving: the deleted benchmark page measured TLS 1.3 keepalive traffic at about 207 RPS for Arc against about 227 RPS for nginx (0.91x), a row the README leaves out.
macOS, Windows without WSL2, or Linux kernels older than 5.10: the data plane needs io_uring.
Anything that depends on nginx configuration, modules, caching or static file serving; Arc has its own config schema and feature set.
Decisions based on the README numbers alone: they are first-party, from a 2-vCPU WSL2 VM with load generator, proxy and backend sharing the cores, and no raw runs are published.

integration.form: standalone binary (Rust workspace, crate arc-gateway; prebuilt Linux x86_64 and arm64 release assets via install.sh)
integration.dependencies: Linux io_uring (kernel 5.10+, 6.1+ recommended); crates rustls/tokio-rustls, hyper, tokio, serde_json/toml/serde_yaml, arc-swap, Wasmtime (plugins); Redis 6+ optional for global rate limiting; XDP needs eBPF support
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (CI builds with stable Rust; workspace crates use edition 2021)
integration.platforms: Linux x86_64 and arm64 only (WSL2 works); no macOS
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable (server process); each worker thread owns its ring, buffers and connection slab, and config hot reload swaps an ArcSwap snapshot
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same reverse-proxy role as nginx proxy_pass, but a different configuration format and no nginx module, cache or static-file ecosystem

gotchas: Benchmark harness: the README table comes from docs/benchmarks.md, deleted in commit ce78a49 (2026-03-02). That page used an nginx static 64-byte backend, wrk -t4 on the same 2-vCPU host and 'the same number of worker processes/threads', and Arc ran with routing, a high rate limit and a no-op plugin. The shipped script (benchmark/scripts/run_h1_wrk_vs_nginx.sh) differs: a Python HTTP/1.0 backend that closes every upstream connection, wrk -t8, ARC_WORKERS=1 against nginx worker_processes auto, and a zero-error gate that checks only non-2xx responses, not wrk socket errors. The deleted page also had rows the README omits: HTTP/2 multiplexing 7,200 vs 6,984 RPS (1.03x) and TLS about 207 vs 227 RPS (0.91x). Its HTTP/2 success-rate row (100% vs 91.5%) was at 32 clients and 10 streams, while the current H2 script defaults to 64 and 20. The Arc RPS figures are identical in its nginx and Pingora tables, so one Arc run was reused against both baselines.

Upstream keep-alive handling (from reading the code, no failure was measured): when an upstream response is not keep-alive, for example an HTTP/1.0 reply without 'Connection: keep-alive' like the bundled Python backend's, worker.rs injects 'Connection: keep-alive' into the client response and sets resp_keepalive. That same flag drives should_checkin_upstream_keepalive, so a socket the upstream is about to close goes back into the idle pool. Only an EPOLLRDHUP watcher drained before checkout evicts it, and the code comment calls that a way 'to reduce stale-conn reuse window'.

Documentation and code disagree: the README Quick Start arc.yaml (node/listeners/discovery schema, 'plugins: {}') does not match arc-config's ConfigFile, which requires top-level listen, admin_listen, workers, io_uring, buffers, timeouts_ms, upstreams, a plugins list and routes. That file would fail to load, so use the arc.example.json schema. docs/benchmarks/index.mdx also documents a PAYLOAD_BYTES variable and random ports, but the script hard-codes --payload-bytes 2 and fixed ports.

Most of the data plane is one 11,675-line worker.rs with 64 unsafe blocks over raw io_uring bindings and manual buffer copies (for example the header injection above). The docs site arc.sdjz.wiki did not resolve, so the in-repo docs are the only reference.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (tokio-uring, vanilla, zix, zeemo, libxev and others in HttpArena) are origin HTTP servers measured on a shared multi-core harness with published configs, whereas Arc is a reverse proxy/gateway measured only by its author. Pick Arc only when you specifically need an io_uring proxy with gateway features in front of other servers, and plan to benchmark it yourself.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README table on a WSL2 Debian VM with 2 vCPU: HTTP/1.1 proxy 102,203 vs 49,930 RPS at 256 connections (2.05x) and 96,143 vs 41,740 RPS at 512 (2.30x), HTTP/2 success 100% vs 91.5%, and added latency +0.82 ms vs +1.35 ms over a 1.18 ms direct path. Per the deleted methodology page, the backend was a static 64-byte nginx and wrk -t4 shared the host. CPU model, nginx version and build, nginx config and raw outputs are not published, and the shipped benchmark script uses a different backend and settings.
status_note: Apache-2.0 and buildable, but an 11-commit, 8-star project last committed 2026-03-11 (two v0.1.x releases), so treat it as experimental rather than an nginx replacement.
